title: Rental renovation licensing by-law approved without tenant compensation
subtitle: Also: development charges debt shift to Cowan gymnasium, heritage designations, advisory committee overhaul, and Lee Brice concert objections.
overview: Council approved a Rental Renovation Licensing By-law, with fees and two new full-time staff positions to run it. The by-law takes effect on the staff-proposed timeline, since a request for an earlier start found no seconder. Council rejected a deferral to the 2027 budget {{vote:m4}}. It lowered the proposed tenant moving payment {{vote:m5}}, then defeated the full compensation amendment {{vote:m6}}. The by-law therefore passed without any tenant compensation.

Council also moved $19,058,000 of development charges debt to the Cowan Recreation Centre gymnasium, extended the Development Charges By-law by up to five years, and started heritage designation steps for several properties. It approved new advisory committee terms of reference effective November 15, 2026, an election-year policy on use of city resources, and a call for a provincial heritage housing grant. After a closed session, Council authorized the Chief Financial Officer to sign a settlement of a development charge complaint.
Two notices of motion on Victoria Street traffic and Kitchener Central Transit Hub communications were deferred to the April 20 special meeting. The meeting ran past midnight.

decisions.detail: Council approved the by-law requiring licences for renovations that need a tenant to vacate, along with its fees and two additional full-time staff positions.
An amendment to require tenant compensation, including moving costs, was defeated {{vote:m6}}, so the by-law has no compensation requirement.
Council reallocated $19,058,000 of development charges debt from the Upper Hidden Valley pumping station and forcemain to the Cowan Recreation Centre gymnasium, with matching reserve fund transfers.
Council amended By-law 2022-071 to extend its term by up to five years.
Council asked the Province to create a $10 million per year grant for housing units within heritage buildings and to circulate the resolution widely.
Council approved, amended and repealed advisory committee terms of reference effective November 15, 2026, and directed staff to report back in 2027 on modernizing the committee model.
Council approved a policy on use of corporate resources for campaign purposes during an election year and amended the Council expense reimbursement policy.
Council agreed to pursue designation under the Ontario Heritage Act for five properties identified in the Bill 23 register review.

debate: Supporters of the rental renovation by-law said bad-faith evictions are hard to challenge at the Landlord and Tenant Board, and that compensation removes the financial incentive to evict. They cited Hamilton's reported drop in filings and said seniors and long-term tenants are most affected.

Opponents, mostly landlords and property managers, argued the by-law duplicates provincial law, adds cost and red tape for small landlords, and may discourage investment and renovations. Many said the Landlord and Tenant Board should be fixed instead.

Councillors favouring deferral to the 2027 budget cited expected budget pressure, lower assessment growth, competing priorities such as snow clearing and potholes, and the view that this is a provincial responsibility. Others said the cost was small, the issue had been before Council for years, and the Province was not acting.

Staff said no legislation prevents the by-law. They noted that compensation goes beyond the Residential Tenancies Act and that similar by-laws elsewhere have not been in force long enough to be tested. Staff also said program costs could exceed the estimate.

On the debt reallocation, a resident argued sewage infrastructure should take priority over a gymnasium. Councillors replied that the debt was already issued and the pumping station project was deferred. Moving it avoids holding unused borrowed money.

Delegations about an April 25 concert at the Memorial Auditorium asked Council to cancel it and review event booking policies, citing the We All Belong Here campaign. Because the item was not on the agenda, Council took no questions or action.
